findings: The frozen Canonical contains two equivalent source variants asking for the definition of a covering index. The candidate answers that intent directly before expanding into mechanism and operational boundaries.

The definition is source-aligned and query-relative: an index covers a particular query when the column information needed from the table can be obtained from that index without an additional row lookup. The answer does not incorrectly present covering index as a separate physical index type or a permanent property of an index.

The InnoDB explanation is correctly bounded to the storage engine: secondary-index records contain the primary-key value, so a secondary index can sometimes provide a selected primary-key column even when that column is not explicitly named in the secondary-index definition.

The candidate correctly separates covering from leftmost-prefix search usability. This avoids the common error of treating efficient search-prefix matching and index-only result retrieval as the same property.

The EXPLAIN boundary is accurate and important: traditional Extra 'Using index' denotes index-only column retrieval, while 'Using index condition' denotes Index Condition Pushdown and can still involve reading full rows. The two are not used as synonyms.

The answer includes relevant operational boundaries from the frozen primary-source packet: prefix indexes cannot automatically be assumed to contain a complete selected string value; wider indexes have storage and write-maintenance costs; and the actual optimizer choice should be verified with EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than assumed.

No unsupported production QPS, latency improvement percentage, I/O reduction figure, schema size or personal project claim is fabricated. The project section explicitly frames a verification workflow because the source contains no real project facts.

The one-minute section now has five main points and is suitable for oral recall. The three-minute section is deliberately thorough and may run longer than a literal three-minute delivery, so oral quality is scored 4/5 rather than 5/5; this is not a promotion-blocking semantic defect.
